opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the most exciting times to be doing ML systems research, but also one of the most challenging, for a few reasons.

The first is scale. A few years ago, a student with a couple of GPUs could build something like a new compiler pass or a new training framework and show meaningful results. Today a lot of the most visible problems, like training frontier models or serving them to millions of users, happen at a scale most universities can't touch. So students sometimes feel the "real" problems are only happening inside big companies. I understand that feeling, but I don't fully agree with it.

That connects to the second challenge, which is choosing the right problem. When the field moves this fast, it's tempting to chase whatever is hot this month, like a new attention variant or a new serving trick, and optimize it by ten percent. Industry teams with many engineers will often do that faster than you can. Academic systems research has its biggest impact when it finds a new abstraction or a new way of thinking that others can build on. A lot of what we did with TVM, XGBoost, and MLC came from asking: what is the reusable layer here? How do we make this work across many kinds of hardware, not just the biggest cluster? Things like running models efficiently on phones, in browsers, or on diverse accelerators turned out to matter a lot, and you don't need a giant data center to work on them.

The third challenge is breadth. To do good ML systems work now, you need to understand the models, the algorithms, the compilers, the hardware, and increasingly the whole stack from kernels to how people actually deploy and use these systems. That's a lot to learn. My advice is to go deep in at least one layer, so you have real technical strength, but stay curious about the layers above and below. Many of the best opportunities sit at the boundaries.

And finally, I'd encourage students to build real things and put them out in the open. Open source has been a big part of my own journey. When you build something people actually use, you get feedback from the real world, you learn what matters, and you build a community that can carry the work much further than one person could. That's something students can do regardless of compute budget.

So yes, the landscape has changed, and the pressure is real. But I'm optimistic. The demand for people who understand how to make AI efficient, accessible, and deployable everywhere is only growing, and there's still a lot of room for good ideas from academia.

r001.rationale: The response says students once could build a compiler pass or training framework with a few GPUs, but does not attribute that accessibility to accumulated experience or say first-principles building has become relatively accessible.

r002.rationale: The response says there is still room for good academic ideas, but does not state that new problems keep arising even when the field seems to have exhausted its problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the ground is moving faster than it has at any point in my career, and that's both the challenge and the opportunity.

The biggest thing I see students struggling with is scale. Ten years ago you could do meaningful systems work on a single GPU, or even a laptop. You could build a new compiler pass, or a new training trick, and demonstrate it end to end yourself. Today the frontier models are trained on thousands of accelerators, and a lot of the interesting systems problems only show up at that scale. So a student looks at that and asks, how can I possibly contribute when I don't have the compute?

My view is that this framing is a trap. If you define your research as "compete with the labs on the thing they're already doing," you will lose. But the frontier is much wider than training the next biggest model. Think about inference. Think about serving on heterogeneous hardware, running models on phones and edge devices, making the same model work across different vendors' chips. Think about the compiler and runtime layers that nobody at a big lab has time to fix because they're all racing on the same handful of problems. Those are places where a graduate student with good taste and a modest cluster can still move the needle, and the impact is actually very broad, because everyone downstream benefits.

The second challenge is the speed of change. A student starts a project on one architecture and eighteen months later the field has moved on. I tell my students to separate the principle from the artifact. The specific model will be obsolete. The abstraction you built, the way you decomposed the problem, the lesson about what the hardware actually wants, that tends to survive. When I worked on XGBoost or on TVM, the thing I cared about most was never the benchmark number at the time. It was whether the underlying design would still make sense when the workload changed. Mostly it did, and that's why those systems lived longer than the papers.

The third thing, and I think people underrate this, is that systems research now requires you to be genuinely full-stack. You need to understand the models well enough to know what matters, the hardware well enough to know what's possible, and the software layer in between well enough to actually build it. That's a lot. But it's also why this area is so exciting for students. The people who can speak all three languages are rare, and they are the ones who end up shaping what the next generation of infrastructure looks like.

And one more practical point. Open source matters more now, not less. If you build something real and people use it, you learn things no paper review will teach you. The feedback loop with actual users is the best training a systems researcher can get. So my advice is don't wait for permission or for the perfect dataset or the perfect cluster. Pick a problem that a lot of people have, build something that works, put it out there, and iterate. That's how most of the things I'm proud of started.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier single-GPU or laptop projects with today’s scale challenge, but does not say accumulated experience has made building from first principles relatively accessible.

r002.rationale: It identifies opportunities in inference, serving, and systems layers, but does not state that new problems keep arising even when the field’s problems seem exhausted.

astra-6.text:
I think one challenge is deciding which problems are worth working on when the field is changing so quickly. As a student, you might spend a few months building a system, and then the models or hardware assumptions change. So you need to ask: what is the underlying problem that will still matter after this particular technology changes?

For machine-learning systems research, that also means connecting different layers. You need to understand something about the model, the software stack, and the hardware, but you can’t become an expert in everything before starting. The practical approach is to pick a concrete problem, understand it deeply, and collaborate with people who bring complementary expertise.

Access to compute is another challenge. But I wouldn’t equate access to the largest cluster with the ability to do valuable research. There are meaningful questions around efficiency, memory constraints, deployment, and making systems easier to use. The key is finding a setting where you can test your ideas convincingly and being clear about what your results establish.

So my advice would be to build strong fundamentals while staying willing to experiment. Read papers, but also build things. Often, the gap between what you expected a system to do and what it actually does is where a good research question begins.

r001.rationale: The response recommends building things and understanding a concrete problem, but does not say accumulated experience has made building from first principles relatively accessible.

r002.rationale: The response notes that the field changes quickly and asks which problems will remain important, but does not state that new research problems keep arising even when the field seems exhausted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one challenge is that the field moves so quickly that it’s easy for students to feel they’re always behind. There’s a new model, a new hardware platform, or a new framework, and you can spend all your time trying to catch up. But research is about finding a question where your work can make a lasting contribution.

For machine-learning systems, that means asking: What is the bottleneck? What becomes possible if we remove it? And does the idea still matter when the model or the hardware changes? Developing that judgment is difficult, because you need to understand both the machine-learning workload and the systems underneath it.

Access to compute is also a challenge. Students may feel that meaningful research requires resources they don’t have. Large-scale experiments do matter for some questions, but there are also valuable problems in efficiency, memory use, compilation, and making models run under practical constraints. The key is to choose a question you can investigate rigorously with the resources available.

So my advice would be to build strong fundamentals, get your hands dirty building systems, and stay close to real problems. Try to understand why something doesn’t work. That understanding can be a much better starting point for research than simply following whatever is popular this month.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building systems and developing fundamentals, but does not say accumulated experience has made first-principles work relatively accessible.

r002.rationale: It notes that models, hardware, and frameworks change quickly, but does not state that new research problems keep arising even when the field’s problems seem exhausted.
